\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कृशः} (kṛśaḥ)}{कृशः (kṛśaḥ)}]{\sk{कृशः} (kṛśaḥ) — thin}

\label{lesson:SA-C132-krsah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for clear, then the Sanskrit for thick.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कृशः}}
\textbf{\sk{कृशः}} — \emph{kṛśaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}thin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kṛśa} \textquotedblleft{}lean, thin, emaciated\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Rigveda, and is inherited from Indo-European (EtymDB). Pali wore it down to \emph{kisa} \textquotedblleft{}lean\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3441).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]

\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for clear, then the Sanskrit for thick, then say \emph{kṛśaḥ} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वक्रः} (vakraḥ)}{वक्रः (vakraḥ)}]{\sk{वक्रः} (vakraḥ) — crooked}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वक्रः}}
\textbf{\sk{वक्रः}} — \emph{vakraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}crooked\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vakra} \textquotedblleft{}crooked, curved, bent\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Atharvaveda, and CDIAL 11185 sets it under the root √vañc \textquotedblleft{}go crookedly\textquotedblright{}, noting that similar words may be non-Aryan. Pali kept it as \emph{vakka} \textquotedblleft{}crooked\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11185).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{ऋजुः} (ṛjuḥ)}{ऋजुः (ṛjuḥ)}]{\sk{ऋजुः} (ṛjuḥ) — straight}

\label{lesson:SA-C132-rjuh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for thin, then the Sanskrit for crooked.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{ऋजुः}}
\textbf{\sk{ऋजुः}} — \emph{ṛjuḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}straight\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ṛju} \textquotedblleft{}straight, upright, honest\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Rigveda, and is inherited from Indo-European: Latin \emph{rēctus} and English \emph{right} are its cousins (EtymDB). Marathi kept it as \emph{ujū} \textquotedblleft{}straight, honest\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 2448).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{पूर्णः} (pūrṇaḥ)}{पूर्णः (pūrṇaḥ)}]{\sk{पूर्णः} (pūrṇaḥ) — full}

\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for crooked, then the Sanskrit for straight.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पूर्णः}}
\textbf{\sk{पूर्णः}} — \emph{pūrṇaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}full\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pūrṇa} is the past participle of the root √pṝ \textquotedblleft{}fill\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 8339): \textquotedblleft{}filled, full\textquotedblright{}. It is inherited from Indo-European, and Latin \emph{plēnus} (English \emph{plenty}) and Persian \emph{pur} \textquotedblleft{}full\textquotedblright{} are cousins (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{रिक्तः} (riktaḥ)}{रिक्तः (riktaḥ)}]{\sk{रिक्तः} (riktaḥ) — empty}

\label{lesson:SA-C132-riktah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for straight, then the Sanskrit for full.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{रिक्तः}}
\textbf{\sk{रिक्तः}} — \emph{riktaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}empty\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rikta} is the past participle of the root √ric \textquotedblleft{}leave, empty\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10729): \textquotedblleft{}left, emptied\textquotedblright{}. The root is inherited from Indo-European, kin to Latin \emph{linquere} \textquotedblleft{}leave\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), and \emph{rikta} lives on as Hindi \emph{rītā} \textquotedblleft{}empty\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10729).
\end{cousinweb}
